rfc1644.title: T/TCP -- TCP Extensions for Transactions Functional Specification (RFC 1644, Experimental)
rfc1644.author: R. Braden, USC Information Sciences Institute
rfc1644.quote: The 3-way handshake adds an extra RTT (round trip time) to the latency of a transaction. [Section 2, p.3] … If an initial <SYN> segment (i.e., a segment containing a SYN bit but no ACK bit) from a particular client host carries a CC value larger than the corresponding cached value, the monotonic property of CC's ensures that the <SYN> segment must be new and can therefore be accepted immediately. [Section 2.1, p.4] … Security Considerations / Security issues are not discussed in this memo. [p.38] … Author's Address / Bob Braden / University of Southern California / Information Sciences Institute / 4676 Admiralty Way / Marina del Rey, CA 90292
supports: Braden, USC ISI, Marina del Rey
the handshake costs one extra RTT
TAO: cached per-client connection count, SYN data accepted immediately
Security Considerations on page 38 is one sentence long

hannum1996.title: Security Problems Associated With T/TCP (unpublished memo, formatted as an Informational RFC draft; 'Request for Comments: ?')
hannum1996.author: Charles M. Hannum, The NetBSD Project
hannum1996.quote: The 3-way handshake (3WHS) in TCP provides minimal security against spoofing the source IP address, by requiring the client to know the initial send sequence number (ISS) of the server. … Worse, the connection count is even more trivial to predict than the ISS. It is therefore a simple matter to submit one-sided requests to a T/TCP server, possibly spoofing such services as rlogin. … These concerns, combined with the fact that sending a FIN with a SYN clearly violates the processing rules in [STD-007], seem to indicate that T/TCP needs more development before it is ready for general use.
supports: the handshake RTT is what makes source-address spoofing hard
the connection count is easier to predict than the ISS
a spoofed request gets accepted and acted on, untraceably

rfc4614.title: A Roadmap for Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) Specification Documents (RFC 4614)
rfc4614.author: M. Duke, R. Braden, W. Eddy, E. Blanton
rfc4614.quote: RFC 1644 E "T/TCP -- TCP Extensions for Transactions Functional Specification" (July 1994): found defective … Furthermore, T/TCP floundered on the ease of denial-of-service attacks that can result. One idea pioneered by T/TCP lives on in RFC 2140, in the sharing of state across connections.
supports: 'floundered on the ease of denial-of-service attacks'
R. Braden of USC ISI is a listed co-author of the document that says it

rfc6247.title: Moving the Undeployed TCP Extensions RFC 1072, RFC 1106, RFC 1110, RFC 1145, RFC 1146, RFC 1379, RFC 1644, and RFC 1693 to Historic Status (RFC 6247)
rfc6247.author: L. Eggert, Nokia
rfc6247.quote: This document reclassifies several TCP extensions that have never seen widespread use to Historic status. … Per this document, the RFC Editor has changed the status of the following RFCs to Historic [RFC2026]: … [RFC1379] and [RFC1644] on "T/TCP -- Extensions for Transactions Functional Specification" … As mentioned in [RFC4614], the TCP Extensions for Transactions (T/TCP) [RFC1379][RFC1644] are reported to have security issues [DEVIVO].

tfo2011.title: TCP Fast Open
tfo2011.author: Sivasankar Radhakrishnan, Yuchung Cheng, Jerry Chu, Arvind Jain, Barath Raghavan
tfo2011.venue: ACM CoNEXT 2011, December 6-9 2011, Tokyo, Japan (read off the PDF's own copyright footer, not an index)
tfo2011.quote: We address the security issues inherent in allowing data exchange during the three-way handshake, which we mitigate using a security token that verifies IP address ownership. … Based on traffic analysis and network emulation, we show that TCP Fast Open would decrease HTTP transaction network latency by 15% and whole-page load time over 10% on average, and in some cases up to 40%. … T/TCP focuses its effort on combating old or duplicate SYNs, and does not aim to mitigate security vulnerabilities introduced by bypassing 3WHS. … Ultimately its scheme is insecure, as discussed by prior analyses [9, 8].
supports: the 15% HTTP transaction network latency figure, stated in the abstract as a projection from traffic analysis and network emulation, not a measurement of a deployment (peer-reviewed, used in preference to any vendor number)
'a security token that verifies IP address ownership'
TFO's authors name T/TCP's scheme insecure

unverified: That FreeBSD and SunOS shipped T/TCP implementations disabled by default. Widely repeated, but I did not open a release note, man page or sysctl default that states it, so it is not in the prose.

RFC 7413 (TCP Fast Open, 2014) and its often-quoted 4-41% page-load saving. Not opened; the CoNEXT 2011 paper's own 15% / over 10% / up to 40% figures are used instead, per the rule to prefer the peer-reviewed number.
Any record of a T/TCP spoofing attack in the wild. Hannum 1996 and the 1998 Phrack article describe attacks that are possible, not incidents that happened.
de Vivo et al., 'Internet Vulnerabilities Related to TCP/IP and T/TCP', ACM SIGCOMM CCR 29(1), January 1999 - cited by RFC 6247 as [DEVIVO], but paywalled and not opened, so nothing rests on it.
Whether Bob Braden personally reviewed the 'found defective' wording in RFC 4614; he is a listed co-author of that RFC, which is all the prose claims.

Any job title or honorific for Bob Braden beyond what the RFCs print. RFC 1644 signs him 'R. Braden / ISI' and RFC 4614 'R. Braden / USC Information Sciences Institute'; the card now claims no more than that.

RFC 2140 is no longer a live RFC: the RFC Editor info page records it as obsoleted by RFC 9040. RFC 4614's 2006 sentence about the idea living on in RFC 2140 is quoted as the 2006 statement it is; no card claims RFC 2140 is current.
